question: lamontae watched a playtest candidate win on election day with 93% of the vote and called it super unrealistic. Answer with empirical distributions, nationwide, not a single state. (1) For each race type (nonpartisan municipal council and mayor; partisan county office; state house and state senate; statewide executive; U.S. House; U.S. Senate), what is the distribution of the winner's share and of the margin, split by: contested versus uncontested; two candidates versus three or more; incumbent running versus open seat; and district partisanship (safe, lean, competitive)? Give the share of contested races won with more than 70%, 80% and 90%, and say when a 90%+ result is real (token opposition, a write-in, a one-party district). (2) How much can a single campaign season plausibly move a candidate's share: what do field experiments and studies of door-knocking, phone banking, mail and advertising say about persuasion per contact and per dollar, how quickly returns diminish, and what ceiling a finite pool of persuadable voters puts on the total? (3) How do opponents respond: how often do they campaign back, and how does a rival's own activity bound what one campaign can gain? (4) How do turnout and undervotes change the counted share in low-turnout local races?
requestedBy: lamontae, 2026-09-22 at 6:11 p.m. Eastern ('93% is super unrealistic'), filed by the research intake thread

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Its own words: 'No empirical win-share or turnout calibration claimed.' It gives a model shape, not numbers.
The code has a floor per candidate and no ceiling, no diminishing returns and no persuadable pool, so it cannot say what a realistic result is.

title: What vote shares real American elections produce, and how far a campaign can move one
usableAnswer: A table of winner-share and margin distributions (median, 10th and 90th percentile, and the rate of 70%+, 80%+ and 90%+ wins) for each race type and split in (1), with its data source and years; persuasion effect sizes per contact and per dollar with their studies; a stated diminishing-returns shape and persuadable-pool ceiling; and a stated fallback for race types with no data. Mark each figure as measured, synthesized or assumed.
whyItMatters: The game counts the vote as each candidate's campaign support share plus a seeded swing of at most 3.5 points (src/simulation/campaigns.ts evaluateCampaignAwareOutcome, at main 2bf9ba97). Support rises with every outreach session as a transfer from the field, 1.5 basis points per volunteer-minute times a 0.6 to 1.41 draw, with no diminishing returns and no ceiling other than a 1% floor for everyone else (requestedGainBasisPoints and campaign-support.ts SUPPORT_FLOOR_BASIS_POINTS). That arithmetic lets enough doorknocking reach 93%; this is an inference from the code, not yet a reproduced trace of that playtest. The earlier answer on election nights (how-an-election-night-should-come-out, A09) says to reuse a candidate, organization and finite-audience model and supplies no empirical win-share or persuasion figures, so the fix has nothing real to calibrate against.
